title: Efficacy and implementation of augmented reality in healthcare: a scoping review in randomized controlled trials.
source: PubMed · International journal of medical informatics
desc: [International journal of medical informatics] Despite medical advances, significant challenges in routine practice persist, including diagnostic variability from traditional two-dimensional (2D) imaging, surgical risks due to anatomical uncertainty, and poor patient comprehension that contributes to perioperative anxiety. Augmented Reality (AR) offers a solution by overlaying three-dimensional (3D) digital information onto the real-world environment, providing real-time guidance to address these clinical gaps. However, while AR's clinical efficacy is increasingly proven, its practical integration into standard clinical workflows remains fragmented. This study presents a scoping review restricted to RCT-level evidence to systematically map the scope, distinct clinical capabilities, implementation limitations, and ethical frameworks of AR-based healthcare systems. A systematic search was conducted across PubMed and Embase to identify randomized controlled trials involving AR interventions in healthcare. Methodological quality was appraised using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Checklist. A total of 25 Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs) were analyzed and categorized based on clinical domains (education, diagnosis, intervention, and rehabilitation) and their functional roles (delivering or assisting). AR was associated with improvements in surgical precision, reductions in perioperative anxiety and better functional outcomes in rehabilitation. In education, AR 3D models fostered patient engagement and shared decision-making. However, widespread adoption is impeded by technical constraints, physiological side effects like cybersickness, high initial costs, and inherent methodological difficulties in blinding. While AR demonstrates distinct capabilities to enhance clinical interventions and empower patient care, technical, logistical, and ethical hurdles persist. Future research must prioritize seamless interoperability with Electronic Health Records (EHR), integration with Artificial Intelligence (AI) decision support, robust health data architectures, and optimized human-computer interaction (HCI) factor design to prevent exacerbating the socioeconomic digital divide.

title: Benchmark of THReD: Evaluating an LLM Agent and Its Preprocessing Tools for Turning Electronic Health Records into AI-Ready Datasets
desc: LLM agents are increasingly built into data-analysis software, yet little evidence shows how reliably they preprocess clinical data or whether the tools they invoke give correct, reproducible output. We report a benchmark of THReD, a web-based system that turns electronic health record (EHR) extracts into AI-ready datasets through a chat agent whose proposed steps run only after user confirmation. The agent benchmark has 141 tasks (100 templates) in seven categories, including goal-level requests, failure recovery, requests calling for no action, schema variation and prompt injection through the data, on synthetic tables calibrated to a regional health information exchange; success is judged by checks on the produced data. Over 2,550 episodes with Claude Haiku 5.5 in four context configurations, the deployed agent completed 92.7% (95% CI 88.1-96.4) of tasks on its first answer, abstained on every advice request, recovered from every injected fault, and never proposed an action requested by planted text. Without the data profile, completion fell to 58.0%; goal-level requests were hardest (80.6%). Six experiments on real records of two chronic-disease cohorts and on synthetic data at scale validate the tools: 91-92% of inferred patient classes and 99.7-99.8% of inferred vital-sign labels were correct in masked reconstruction; a dictionary builder combining curated dictionaries with LLM suggestions mapped 99.0% of 2,208 raw variants correctly; all 2,176 replays of 128 saved pipelines gave byte-identical files under pinned dependencies; subgroup differences in inference accuracy vanished within facility and lookup key; and the same-day consolidation rule changed 90-day emergency revisit rates by up to 3.2 points without shifting cohort composition by more than one point. Processing time grew roughly linearly to 5.5 million records while the prompt stayed at about 13 thousand tokens.

title: PhenoMe: An interactive AI framework for interpretable, microscopy-driven phenotyping
desc: Extracting meaningful biological patterns from microscopy image datasets requires tools that quantitatively connect visual similarities and experimental context. Deep learning models, and in particular novel foundation models, have the capacity to translate images into high-dimensional embeddings that can better represent complex visual patterns. Using these complex representations analytically and linking them to experimental information, it is possible to build advanced exploratory and phenotyping capabilities. Here, we present PhenoMe, an open-source, model-agnostic framework to handle pretrained foundation model-derived image representations alongside quantitative image properties and experimental metadata. PhenoMe integrates multiple scriptable and interactive workflows for embedding space visualisation, dimensionality reduction and clustering, similarity-based comparison and retrieval of representative images for each phenotype, among others. It also supports correlation analyses that link the embedding structure to interpretable image properties. We demonstrate PhenoMe's capabilities on seven public microscopy datasets, ranging from cell painting assays, nanoscale synaptic images, drug-response analyses and dynamic cell-phenotyping. These case studies show how readily available image representations can support data contextualisation, curation and analysis. Through guided notebooks, reproducible configurations, extensible model wrappers and a napari plugin, PhenoMe makes representation-based microscopy exploration accessible to researchers without dedicated technical expertise. PhenoMe lays the groundwork for applying foundation models and representation learning to microscopy data analysis.

title: Artificial intelligence in healthcare: clinical applications, evidence maturity, risks, and life-cycle governance.
source: PubMed · International journal of medical informatics
desc: [International journal of medical informatics] Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used across clinical, administrative, and public health settings, but technical performance alone does not establish clinical utility, safety, equity, or sustainability. To critically analyze contemporary healthcare AI applications, characterize source types and non-ordinal evidence profiles in the supporting literature, synthesize key opportunities and risks, and identify governance requirements for clinically useful, safe, equitable, and responsible implementation. We conducted a critical narrative synthesis using PubMed, the Virtual Health Library, Web of Science, and Scopus as source-discovery tools on July 16, 2026. A curated corpus of 28 bibliographically verifiable publications was assembled judgmentally to provide complementary coverage of clinical applications, evidence characteristics, implementation, risk, and life-cycle governance. Sources were classified by primary design and non-mutually exclusive evidentiary domains, and the evidence described within them was characterized using non-ordinal profile categories. Findings were synthesized qualitatively because of substantial heterogeneity across technologies, settings, and source designs. The curated corpus addressed diagnosis and imaging, prediction and monitoring, clinical documentation, conversational systems, public health, hospital operations, and specialty applications. Within this assembled corpus, technical-performance/validation and process-utility/workflow domains were represented more often than clinical or patient-safety outcomes, economic outcomes, or post-deployment surveillance; these document-level counts are descriptive and have no inferential weight beyond the selected sources. Reported or proposed benefits included diagnostic support, personalization, documentation, surveillance, and workflow efficiency. Recurrent risks included poor generalizability, bias, miscalibration, hallucinations, opacity, privacy concerns, interoperability problems, inappropriate automation, unclear accountability, and hidden costs. Within this non-exhaustive corpus, the evidence more consistently supported assistive, context-specific uses than generalized autonomous replacement. Responsible implementation requires a clearly defined intended use, governed data, contextual validation, risk-proportionate human oversight, traceability, equity and safety assessment, continuous monitoring, and procedures to restrict, suspend, or withdraw systems when performanc

title: Multidimensional Suicide Risk Assessment with Machine Learning using Electronic Health Records
desc: Suicide prevention remains a critical public health challenge, and electronic health records (EHRs) provide an opportunity to characterize suicide-related risk indicators using documented clinical, behavioral, medical, and social-contextual information. This paper presents a multidimensional machine learning framework to model and estimate suicide-related outcomes using MIMIC-IV EHR data. We construct clinically motivated diagnosis categories and define a composite outcome from documented codes corresponding to suicidal ideation, suicide attempt, prior suicidal behavior, and intentional self-harm. To address severe class imbalance and reduce age-related confounding, we apply age-matched resampling that retains all positive patients and samples comparison-cohort patients from the same age group. Logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost classifiers are evaluated before and after resampling with isotonic calibration. The calibrated XGBoost model achieves the strongest matched-cohort performance, outperforming the other evaluated classifiers. SHAP-based interpretation shows that diagnostic burden, depression-related features, age, personality-disorder history, social determinants related to violence, and medical comorbidity contribute to elevated predicted probabilities. Our results demonstrate that combining broad EHR-derived features, age-matched cohort construction, calibration, and feature-level interpretation provides a practical framework for retrospective suicide-related risk modeling.

title: scSTEC: Annotating Chromatin Subcompartments from Individual Single-Cell Hi-C Data via Direct Two-Dimensional Embedding and Chromosome-wise Consensus
desc: textbf{Motivation: }Single-cell Hi-C (scHi-C) technologies enable the study of three-dimensional (3D) genome organization at individual-cell resolution. Many computational methods have been developed to infer hierarchical structures from scHi-C data. However, annotating chromatin subcompartments from sparse scHi-C data remains a challenge. The recently developed scGHOST provides a framework for single-cell subcompartment annotation, but relies on a deep learning-based architecture, a multi-step upstream pipeline involving cell embedding and matrix imputation, and cross-cell information sharing. These features complicate algorithmic interpretation and make the annotation of an individual cell dependent on information from other cells in the dataset. Hence, methods are needed that annotate subcompartments directly from an individual cell's own contact matrix, without complex upstream processing or cross-cell information sharing. textbf{Results: }We developed scSTEC, a computational framework that annotates subcompartments directly from an individual scHi-C matrix without data imputation, complex upstream processing, or cross-cell data sharing. We show that the estimated inter-chromosomal matrix constructed by scGHOST is intrinsically of rank 2, revealing that the geometry relevant to clustering can be represented in two dimensions. Leveraging this low-dimensional structure, scSTEC performs direct subcompartment annotation through 2D genomic embedding and chromosome-wise consensus. Across bulk Hi-C, downsampled simulations, and real scHi-C datasets (four human cell lines, adult mouse cortex, developing mouse embryos, and developing olfactory sensory neurons), scSTEC achieves subcompartment annotations comparable to scGHOST despite operating on each cell independently, while providing greater algorithmic interpretability. Furthermore, subcompartments identified by scSTEC effectively resolve cell types, capture developmental dynamics, and show consistent associations with gene expression and epigenetic profiles. \textbf{Availability: }scSTEC is freely available at url{https://github.com/Ge-lab-pku/scSTEC}.

Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Nanomedicine in Precision Oncology: Diagnosis, Targeted Therapy, and Clinical Translation.
desc: [International journal of nanomedicine] Cancer nanomedicine offers programmable platforms for diagnosis, imaging, drug and gene delivery, and theranostics, but its clinical performance is constrained by tumor heterogeneity, complex nano-bio interactions, and interpatient variability. Artificial intelligence (AI) provides a means to integrate physicochemical, biological, imaging, molecular, and clinical data to improve the design and application of nanoscale cancer technologies. This Review examines the convergence of AI and nanotechnology across cancer diagnosis, therapeutic selection, treatment optimization, monitoring, drug development, and clinical translation, with particular emphasis on materials design and biological performance. AI-based approaches can support early detection, patient stratification, response and toxicity prediction, and rational therapeutic development. In parallel, nanoplatforms, including liposomes, polymeric nanoparticles, dendrimers, metallic and inorganic nanoparticles, biomimetic systems, and stimuli-responsive carriers, can improve pharmacokinetics, enhance tumor exposure, reduce systemic toxicity, and enable controlled delivery of diverse payloads. Their integration may advance precision nanomedicine by guiding nanoparticle composition, size, surface properties, targeting ligands, biodistribution, tumor accumulation, cellular uptake, protein-corona formation, release kinetics, toxicity, and therapeutic response. Conversely, nanodiagnostic and nanotheranostic systems can generate imaging, molecular, pharmacokinetic, and response data for AI-assisted patient selection and adaptive treatment monitoring. Translation will require standardized datasets, reproducible nanoparticle characterization, scalable manufacturing, explainable and externally validated models, regulatory clarity, long-term safety assessment, and equitable implementation. Together, AI-guided nanotechnology provides a framework linking materials design, biological interactions, and patient-specific cancer therapy.

title: Temporal Island Sparse Autoencoders for Interpreting Clinical Time-Series Models
desc: Deep learning models for electronic health records achieve strong predictive performance but provide little insight into what clinical concepts they represent internally. Post-hoc attribution methods produce per-cell importance scores that lack temporal coherence, cross-variable structure, and reusability across patients. We introduce the Temporal Island Sparse Autoencoder (TI-SAE), which learns a backbone-specific, patient-shared clinical concept dictionary from a frozen predictive model's representations. Each dictionary entry (latent) is defined by learned temporal Gaussian islands (specifying when the concept is active) and a sparse variable-composition vector (specifying which variables are involved). A decoupled selector then identifies which dictionary entries drive each patient's prediction, separating representation learning from attribution. We evaluate TI-SAE across five backbone architectures spanning different representation strategies on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV (three prediction tasks each). TI-SAE produces structured clinical concepts that go beyond transient attribution heatmaps while achieving strong performance on standard faithfulness benchmarks.

title: AI-based structural modelling and pathogenic variant mapping across the human protein interactome
desc: Spanning the complex landscape of the human proteome, physical interactions between proteins coordinate cellular organization, signaling, regulation, and homeostasis. Yet the three-dimensional structures of most of these interactions remain unresolved. Here, we performed AI-based modelling of 109,282 human protein interaction structures, generating a structural resource for large-scale analysis. The predicted structures were systematically characterized through analysis of interface residue involvement, buried surface area, intermolecular bonding, and energetic properties. Additionally, we mapped pathogenic variant data onto the predicted structures, identifying interface-localized mutations for over 4,000 annotated disease categories. Acute myeloid leukemia, Alzheimer's disease, and cardiomyopathy were examined as representative disease contexts for exploring the distribution of interface mutations within disease-associated protein interaction networks. Strengths and limitations of predictive capabilities were also assessed, including through experimental structure comparisons. Collectively, this structural resource and accompanying analyses offer a basis for developing novel hypotheses and informing experimental studies involving human protein interactions in physiological and disease contexts.

title: Artificial intelligence assisted genomic profiling of ovarian cancer liver metastases.
desc: [Frontiers in genetics] Liver involvement in ovarian cancer is often treated as a single clinical entity, although liver-surface implants and parenchymal deposits occupy different anatomical settings and may not share the same molecular history. Primary-tumor profiling is informative, but can miss lesion-specific evolution, treatment-associated cell states, and microenvironmental structure. This Mini Review examines how germline susceptibility, somatic change, spatial biology, and artificial intelligence might be combined in high-grade serous ovarian cancer. The central task is not simply outcome prediction. It is to distinguish constitutional from tumor-acquired variation, retain lesion identity and treatment timing, and relate molecular programs to defined spatial compartments. Current data support marked clonal and microenvironmental heterogeneity in ovarian cancer, but direct molecular evidence from hepatic lesions remains sparse. AI-based integration is therefore best viewed as a way to formulate and test reproducible hypotheses, rather than as a validated route to select liver-directed therapy. Paired sampling, orthogonal assays, patient-level validation, and decision-specific clinical endpoints will be needed before these models can influence management.

title: Findings-aware Language-Image Pretraining for CT Volume Interpretation
desc: Computed tomography (CT) provides diverse patient information and various clinical tasks, for which numerous deep learning models have been investigated. Recent years have seen the development of vision-language foundation models that can comprehensively extract clinical features, driven by representation learning that combines CT volumes with radiology reports. Existing approaches typically adopt Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP)-based representation learning, where pairs from different cases are, in principle, treated as negative pairs such that the volume and report embeddings are pushed apart. In the biomedical imaging, however, treating different cases as negative pairs is not always appropriate, particularly when clinical similarity exists. In this study, we propose a supervised representation learning framework grounded in clinical knowledge from language foundation models, rather than the weak supervision used in CLIP. Specifically, we utilized a large language model to extract abnormal finding phrases from reports. We then explicitly constructed the target features that the image encoder should output, as the semantic representation of the extracted findings using a biomedical text embedding model. Our Findings-aware Language-Image Pre-training (FiLIP) outperformed weakly supervised approaches in multi-label zero-shot finding classification in both in-domain and external-domain evaluations, and also proved effective when fine-tuned for the downstream task of radiology report generation.

title: VIGAT: VLM-guided gene activity quantification from single-cell ATAC-seq
desc: Summary: Gene activity quantification from single-cell ATAC-seq is challenging because genomic regions informative of cell identity can vary across genes and tissues, while broadly accessible regions may provide limited cell-type-discriminative information. We developed VIGAT, a vision-language model (VLM)-guided tool that automates visual interpretation of ATAC coverage plots for adaptive gene activity quantification. VIGAT jointly examines accessibility patterns across multiple marker genes, integrating genomic annotations and biological context to select gene-specific regions enriched for cluster-discriminative signals. Selected regions are used to generate a gene-by-cell activity matrix. Across 196 paired single-cell RNA-seq and ATAC-seq datasets, VIGAT outperformed five existing methods in recovering marker-associated accessibility enriched in the corresponding cell populations, demonstrating the utility of VLM-guided visual reasoning for scalable gene activity quantification. Availability and implementation: VIGAT is implemented as an open-source R package and is freely available at https://github.com/beijie02/VIGAT.

Immunity and inflammation in classic Hodgkin lymphoma: Bridging diagnosis, prognosis and precision medicine.
desc: [Blood reviews] Classic Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is a unique B-cell malignancy characterized by a small number of malignant Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg (HRS) cells embedded within an extensive and highly organized inflammatory microenvironment. Recent studies have highlighted that the biological behavior of cHL is largely determined by dynamic interactions between HRS cells and surrounding immune populations, including CD4+ T cells, regulatory T cells, macrophages, eosinophils, mast cells, natural killer cells, and stromal elements. HRS cells actively reshape the tumor microenvironment through the secretion of chemokines and cytokines, including CCL17, CCL22, IL-6, IL-10, and TGF-β, promoting immune cell recruitment, chronic inflammation, and immune tolerance. Concurrently, genetic alterations affecting the PD-1/PD-L1 axis, antigen-presentation pathways, and key signaling cascades such as NF-κB and JAK/STAT facilitate immune escape and tumor persistence. We distinguish diagnostic, prognostic, predictive, and response-monitoring applications and grade biomarkers as established (immunophenotyping, EBER, clinical scores, interim PET), clinically promising (serum TARC, circulating tumor DNA), or investigational (PD-L1-based prediction, spatial and single-cell profiling, artificial intelligence). A deeper understanding of the interplay between immunity and inflammation in cHL may refine disease classification and guide the development of novel immunomodulatory strategies aimed at improving long-term outcomes and overcoming resistance to current therapies.

title: Accuracy Is Not Risk: Why Medical AI Should Not Report Only Its Most Likely Label
desc: Background. Many medical AI models are trained to reproduce a single reference label and hand the most likely label to the next step in a clinical workflow. A classifier can select that label correctly while providing an inadequate summary for estimating downstream risk. Methods. We use Jeffrey's rule of conditioning to specify when probabilities over intermediate states, such as diagnoses or imaging categories, can be carried forward to an outcome risk. We separate two errors of reporting only the most likely label, discarding the probability of the other states and applying the risk of patients who have the leading diagnosis to a patient who only probably has it. We also give conditions under which the label and the full distribution lead to the same decision, and we propose guardrails for device developers, regulatory reviewers, and health insurers. Results. In a hypothetical chest-pain differential, reporting only the benign leading diagnosis greatly understates the patient's risk of death or cardiac arrest, so a patient who warrants evaluation could be discharged or denied imaging. In a hypothetical BI-RADS example, the most likely category is "probably benign," yet the propagated malignancy risk exceeds the ceiling that defines that category. Conclusions. A predicted label is not an observed state, and a calibrated classifier is not automatically a valid outcome model. Clinical and insurance coverage decisions should rest on the patient's outcome risk, judged against a threshold justified by the consequences of acting and not acting. Developers should state what each model output means and check that every step between the model and the decision preserves the patient's risk.

title: BioResearchBench: 50 Long Horizon Biological Research Tasks
desc: AI models are used in biology research to study disease mechanisms, discover potential treatments, analyze experimental data, troubleshoot problems, and plan next steps. Useful assistance depends on working with data in various scientific formats, interpreting results, and deciding what to test next. We present BioResearchBench, a benchmark of 50 research questions developed by PhD biologists drawing on their deep research expertise to reflect realistic problems encountered in their fields. Questions were refined through expert review and iterative model testing. The collection spans 10 diverse biology subdomains and includes sequencing data, proteomic measurements, microscopy images, assay readouts, and clinical datasets. We compared recorded outcomes and examined model responses in depth across the 50 tasks on OpenAI GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 4 Argon, Meta Muse Wonder, and SpaceXSI Grok 4.7. Success across our benchmark was 18% for Claude Opus 5.5, 13% for Gemini 4 Argon, 11% for Meta Muse Wonder, 4% for GPT-6 Astra, and 4% for Grok 4.7. These results describe a deliberately challenging collection selected through expert review and model testing. Despite low whole task success, the selected responses met most rubric requirements on average: the average fraction of criteria missed ranged from 18% to 32% across models. Across models, the proportion of eligible tasks with at least one category failure was highest in computation and data handling (66.9% failure), followed by uncertainty and identification (55.3% failure), reporting and completeness (54.7% failure), biological interpretation (39.0% failure), controls and causal claims (37.2% failure), and choosing the next experiment or decision (31.0% failure). Gemini 4 Argon had the highest proportion of reviewed tasks without a recorded category failure in computation and data handling (45% success) and biological interpretation (69% success). Claude Opus 5.5 led in controls and causal claims (72% success) and choosing the next experiment or decision (75% success). GPT-6 Astra led in uncertainty and identification (56% success) which included judging the precision of estimates and recognizing when measurements could not distinguish between biological explanations. GPT-6 Astra and Meta Muse Wonder tied for the highest proportion of answers with no recorded omissions or reporting failures (51% success). Assessment, intervention, and ethical considerations of artificial intelligence for depression and suicide risk: A scoping review.
desc: [Psychiatry research] Depression and suicidal behavior constitute leading causes of global disease burden. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers promise for improving detection, intervention, and prevention, yet no comprehensive review has simultaneously mapped AI-driven assessment, intervention, and ethical considerations across both conditions. To systematically map AI applications for depression and suicide risk across three thematic axes: (1) assessment and diagnosis, (2) conversational AI and AI-driven interventions, and (3) ethical, equity, and regulatory considerations, and to evaluate translational maturity using a novel framework. Following JBI scoping review methodology and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, six databases were searched from January 2020 through March 2026. Two independent reviewers screened 5079 records using a two-stage process, yielding 2844 included studies (Cohen's kappa = 0.66). Data were extracted using a standardized charting form with AI-assisted full-text analysis. Assessment/diagnosis dominated (n = 1785), with fewer intervention studies (n = 318). Large language model-related studies rose from <1% (2020-2022) to 11.1% (2025) of included studies annually. Translational Readiness Framework classification revealed 44.8% Laboratory, 49.2% Bridge, and 6.0% Clinical stage, with intervention studies showing the highest Clinical-stage proportion (16.7% vs. 5.9% for assessment). Five cross-cutting observations emerged, including an inverted evidence pyramid and persistent cross-axis integration gap (4.4%). Despite technical advances, the evidence base remains concentrated at early translational stages. The proposed Translational Readiness Framework provides a structured lens for evaluating progress and guiding research prioritization. Closing the gap between laboratory promise and clinical impact requires a shift from model-centric to patient-centric research and from benchmark performance to real-world validation.

title: Conversational Interaction for LLM-Based Clinical Text-to-SQL: A User Study with Healthcare Professionals
desc: Conversational text-to-SQL interfaces could give healthcare professionals natural-language access to electronic health record (EHR) data, but evidence for their real-world usability remains limited: prior evaluations have relied largely on curated benchmarks with fully specified questions or on simulated users. We report a user study in which 14 physicians who regularly work with EHR data used both a single-turn and a conversational multi-turn text-to-SQL interface over the MIMIC-IV database in a within-subjects design; dialogue analyses additionally drew on interaction logs from 21 healthcare professionals across the main study and two pilot studies. The conversational interface was consistently favored: mean System Usability Scale scores rose from 68.2, near the industry average, to 85.9 (p<0.001), with significant advantages across technology-acceptance constructs including performance expectancy, effort expectancy, self-efficacy, and behavioral intention. In post-study forced-choice comparisons, 93% of participants reported greater overall satisfaction with the conversational interface, 86% preferred it for real-world adoption, and 71% trusted its results more; no participant preferred or trusted the single-turn interface more. Turn-level analysis of 425 logged user turns showed that freely composed queries triggered clarification requests in 24.8% of cases versus 1.8% for predefined, fully specified questions, and 64.3% of clarification episodes stemmed from EHR- or clinical-domain knowledge. Conversational interaction is a practical prerequisite, rather than a convenience, for natural-language EHR access. The frequent need for clarification in realistic clinical queries further underscores the importance of conversational interfaces, while benchmark-style evaluation can substantially underrepresent the ambiguity of real clinical use.

title: FedEpitope: Parameter-Efficient Federated Protein Language Models for Linear B-Cell Epitope Prediction
desc: Linear B-cell epitopes are antigenic regions recognised by antibodies that play crucial roles in vaccine development, antibody production, and other therapeutic applications.Their prediction can support peptide-based vaccine candidate screening and diagnostic assay development, but the experimental data required for model development may be distributed across institutions that cannot freely pool their records. We present FedEpitope, a federated framework that adapts the ESM-2 protein language model for peptide-level linear B-cell epitope prediction using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), keeping client-partitioned data local and restricting the communicated trainable model state to approximately 1.11 MB. Simulated benchmarks of FedAvg and FedProx algorithms, evaluated using homology-aware data splits of five biologically heterogeneous, organism-partitioned clients, achieve promising global test performance without centralising training data, with FedAvg outperforming all single-client models in mean AP, F1, and MCC. Additional experiments characterise post-federation personalisation, record-level differential privacy, sensitivity to controlled client heterogeneity, LoRA rank, and generalisation to the independent BCPreds and NetBCE benchmarks, demonstrating the feasibility of parameter-efficient federated protein language model adaptation for data-localised B-cell epitope prediction and the associated trade-offs among predictive performance, personalisation, privacy, communication efficiency, and distribution shift.

Outcomes of informal and formal care models at the end of life: An AI-supported systematic review.
desc: [Geriatric nursing (New York, N.Y.)] Multimorbidity and functional decline become increasingly prevalent with age, particularly in those near the end of life. This poses critical challenges for both families and society in providing adequate care. However, it remains unclear which type of care yields better outcomes. To systematically assess the impact of informal care, formal care, and a combination of both on health outcomes, healthcare utilization, and costs of care for older adults near the end of life. A systematic review with narrative synthesis was registered on PROSPERO (CRD42024512003). Screening was assisted by machine learning tool ASReview, and study quality was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool, with support from large language model TXYZ.AI. Articles published between database inception and June 4th, 2025 were identified in PubMed, Embase, and CINAHL. Thirty-six studies, including 20 observational and 16 interventional were included. Most observational studies examined place of death, with some associations involving informal care pointing towards lower home death or greater hospital death. In contrast, physician and nurse home visits were associated with a greater likelihood of home death. Specialized formal care interventions generally reported improvements in quality of life and reductions in healthcare use. Quality assessment showed 85.2% AI-human agreement, with 44.4% of studies meeting all seven quality criteria. Informal care did not necessarily facilitate home death, whereas formal home-based care was linked to a greater likelihood of home death. Interventional evidence also suggests broader benefits of specialized formal care, although certainty was limited by methodological concerns.

title: Accessed, never disclosed: Silent access to protected health information by medical artificial intelligence agents
desc: Medical artificial intelligence agents should retrieve patient identifiers only when a task requires them, the data-minimization principle behind the HIPAA minimum necessary standard for protected health information (PHI). An agent can retrieve identifiers without revealing them. Such silent access remains invisible to evaluations that inspect only the output. We embedded canaries in synthetic patient records and linked each tool invocation to canary exposure in the final answers across five language models, four boundary levels, and seven attack frames for identifier-free clinical tasks. Three models invoked the PHI tools unnecessarily, whereas Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 did not. Stronger boundaries reduced this access, and the residual access under the strictest policy was confined to frames in which the user overrode the policy or asserted approval. A pre-execution gate given the task-necessity criterion nearly eliminated this access. Output-only evaluation cannot verify minimum-necessary access; boundaries, gates, and access-log audits are required together.

title: Unsupervised prioritization of gene-regulatory variants with isolation forests
desc: Most common variants occur in non-coding genomic regions. Numerous expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) can influence nearby gene expression. Across diverse traits and diseases, many genome-wide association study (GWAS) loci have been shown to colocalize with eQTLs, supporting gene-regulatory causal mechanisms. However, linkage disequilibrium (LD) obscures the identification of the causal variant(s), necessitating prioritization by functional annotations. Previously published variant prioritization tools relied on the machine-learning-based combination of diverse feature types like evolutionary conservation and chromatin information, whereas more recent deep learning tools learn and describe gene-regulatory DNA sequence grammar. However, the latter approaches often generate a large number of scores per variant. We designed a novel unsupervised machine-learning approach based on isolation forests to integrate the predictions from the broadly used Enformer deep learning model into a single gene-regulatory predictive score for each common variant. Our novel approach eQTL prediction with isolation forests (eQIF) demonstrates strong performance in predicting eQTLs and gene-regulatory GWAS variants. We show that top eQIF variants are located in evolutionarily conserved transcription factor binding site (TFBS) footprints, and that the frequency of top eQIF variants within overrepresented TFBS motifs recapitulates the motif information content. eQIF predictions are precomputed for 9,431,969 common variants and publicly available.

title: Stakeholders offer competing feedback on how FDA should regulate genAI devices
Artificial intelligence for video-based assessment of surgical performance in robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery in real operative settings: a systematic review.
source: PubMed · International journal of medical informatics
desc: [International journal of medical informatics] Robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery requires specific skills of the surgeon beyond the mastery of conventional laparoscopic techniques. However, efficient and objective methods for evaluating these skills remain limited. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers potential for a more objective, video-based performance assessment. This systematic review aims to evaluate the current evidence of using AI for evaluation of surgical skill in real robotic surgery and outline potential avenues for future research. We systematically searched Ovid Medline, Embase, Clarivate Web of Science, ERIC Institute of Education Sciences and Scopus databases from inception to 10 July 2025, for studies evaluating AI-based technical skill assessment using videos of robot-assisted surgery performed on real patients. Study characteristics, AI approaches, assessment targets, reference standards, and model performance were extracted. Risk of bias and applicability were assessed using PROBAST + AI. Owing to differences in assessment constructs and reported performance measures, findings were synthesised using a structured narrative approach. In total, 2116 articles were identified, of which 5 met our eligibility criteria. AI approaches and assessment targets varied substantially across studies, including prediction of global technical skill scores, analysis of instrument-derived performance metrics, procedure-specific assessment, and surgical error detection. Reference standards included OSATS, GEARS or modified GEARS, PLACE, and procedural experience. Reported performance measures represented different constructs and were not directly comparable across studies. PROBAST + AI identified important methodological limitations, and no study reported external validation using an independent dataset. AI shows potential for video-based technical skill assessment in real robotic surgery, but current evidence is limited and heterogeneous. Future research should prioritise standardised annotation, multicentre intraoperative datasets, and external validation to support reliable translation into clinical practice.

title: MedPsy: State-of-the-Art Small Medical Language Models for Efficient Edge Deployment
desc: Medical language models promise expert clinical support, but the strongest open-source LLMs remain too large for private edge-device deployment, while compact medical models still trail substantially on knowledge-intensive and real-world healthcare tasks. Reasoning models that fit edge memory budgets can produce long reasoning traces, increasing sequential decoding, end-to-end latency, energy consumption, and KV-cache memory pressure. We present MedPsy, a family of text-only 1.7B and 4B medical language models designed for edge deployment, targeting this accuracy-generation-efficiency trade-off. Our recipe combines a synthetic medical data pipeline over biology, medicine, and health seeds with chain-of-thought targets from a 235B medical-focused LLM teacher; a four-stage post-training curriculum comprising two SFT stages followed by two RL stages with hard-sample mining; and an edge deployment evaluation spanning multiple GGUF quantization variants and real-device inference on laptop and smartphone hardware. On seven closed-ended medical benchmarks, MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-1.5-4B by 19.34 points and matches MedGemma-27B while being 6.75x smaller; MedPsy-1.7B outperforms MedGemma-1.5-4B by 11.42 points despite being less than half its size. On HealthBench-Hard, MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-27B by 15.33 points, while MedPsy-1.7B surpasses it by 11.66 points despite being ~16x smaller. Beyond accuracy, MedPsy reduces average response length by 1.7x (1.7B) and 3.2x (4B) versus its Qwen3 backbones, while Q4_K_M quantization preserves the aggregate score within 1 point of BF16 with ~69% lower disk footprint. In real-device inference, MedPsy-4B's shorter generations translate into 75% lower median end-to-end latency and estimated energy per answer than its Qwen3 backbone at matched quantization, while peak RAM remains below 5 GB across our tested laptop and smartphone configurations.

title: DEEPNET-LLM: Highly accurate structure prediction of unknown metabolites from mass spectra via their molecular neighborhoods
desc: Most molecular features detected by untargeted mass spectrometry-based metabolomics remain unannotated. This so-called 'dark matter' currently comprises more than 90% and likely holds uncharacterized bioactive chemistry. Structure prediction from fragmentation spectra remains an outstanding challenge, because a spectrum does not uniquely determine a structure and the space of candidate structures is mostly unbounded; correspondingly, existing methods rarely return the correct de novo structure as their top prediction. Here we describe De novo Ego network-Enabled Propagation and Neighborhood Extrapolation of Topology using Large Language Models (DEEPNET-LLM) reasoning approach, which uses Molecular Community Networking (MCN) to restrict the search of a query spectrum to its local neighborhood within the global metabolome, and applies AI reasoning to propagate structural information from neighbors to the query. For a collection of 900 authentic standards (2,249 spectra) that have never been publicly released to exclude possibility of data leakage, DEEPNET-LLM returned the correct structure as its top prediction for 84.7% of spectra. Accuracy was independent of precursor mass across a range over which the number of candidate structures grows by 30 orders of magnitude, and was comparable across ion polarity, adducts and in-source fragmentation. On a random subset of the public MassSpecGym benchmark, DEEPNET-LLM reached 85.9% top-1 accuracy excluding stereochemistry. We showcase the use of DEEPNET-LLM with an example of a discovery of tryptamine amidate of a bile acid in mouse gut, confirmed against a synthetic standard. The DEEPNET-LLM approach is orthogonal to existing in silico methods and can be combined with them.

title: FDA Selects Initial Devices for Home Innovation Challenge
Artificial Intelligence in Laryngology: Applications for Voice, Swallowing, and Endoscopic Assessment.
source: PubMed · ORL-head and neck nursing : official journal of the Society of Otorhinolaryngology and Head-Neck Nurses
desc: [ORL-head and neck nursing : official journal of the Society of Otorhinolaryngology and Head-Neck Nurses] Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into otolaryngology-head and neck care, with rapid growth in laryngology due to its reliance on voice analysis, endoscopic imaging, and swallowing assessment. As AI tools move into routine practice, otolaryngology teams play a key role in ensuring ethical, effective, and patient-centered implementation. To describe current and emerging applications of AI in laryngology with direct relevance to otolaryngology-head and neck care. A narrative review of the peer-reviewed literature was conducted, focusing on clinically relevant and investigational AI applications in laryngology care. Areas of emphasis included voice disorders and dysphagia, with attention to nursing, speech language pathology, and surgical practice. AI applications in laryngology care span multiple domains, including automated voice analysis for screening and monitoring, AI-assisted interpretation of laryngoscopy and swallowing studies, noninvasive dysphagia screening using sound or wearable sensors, and tools to support documentation and clinical triage. Collectively, these technologies can improve diagnostic consistency, support earlier identification of complications, and enhance longitudinal monitoring across care settings. Effective integration of AI into laryngeal care requires coordinated team engagement in data analysis, patient education, and clinical decision support. Understanding AI capabilities and limitations is essential for improving care while mitigating bias and supporting efficient workflows. AI-enabled technologies have expanded data-driven laryngology care across voice, swallowing, and endoscopic evaluation. Successful adoption depends on data quality, performance, and workflow integration. Interdisciplinary collaboration and ongoing evaluation of safety and equity can enhance the quality and consistency of laryngeal care.

title: Deep Learning for Cervical Cytology Screening: Methods, Algorithms, Challenges and Prospects
desc: Cervical cancer remains a leading cause of cancer death among women, with more than 90\% of deaths occurring in low- and middle-income countries, where cytology screening is constrained by a shortage of trained cytopathologists. Deep learning has made automated cytology screening increasingly feasible, but the literature is fragmented across cell, patch and whole-slide-image scales, task formulations and supervision regimes, hindering comparison and clinical translation. This Review synthesizes the deep learning literature for cervical cytology screening, organizing the field along three axes---data scale, functional task and supervision---and distinguishing two clinical roadmaps: whole-slide-image confidence aggregation and cell-level detection with Bethesda classification. We examine 16 publicly available or publicly documented cytology datasets alongside the CAISHI histopathology dataset, compare quantitative performance while exposing incomparable metrics and data leakage, and assess commercial systems, regulatory status, HPV-era screening pathways and low-resource deployment. Single-cell accuracy on Herlev and SIPaKMeD has plateaued, but this reflects benchmark saturation rather than clinical readiness; prospective and randomized evidence is emerging but remains limited. We consolidate the evidence into five challenge areas---data and benchmarks, architecture and label-efficient learning, trustworthy AI, clinical translation and health economics, and evaluation and reproducibility---and provide an evidence-to-agenda map and a deployment decision matrix. Progress now depends on multi-center benchmarks, externally validated label-efficient methods, calibrated and fair predictions, and pragmatic clinical trials rather than further gains on saturated single-cell benchmarks.

title: Improving real-time search through deep learning-enhanced fragment ion indexing
desc: The fragment ion indexed database searching approach enables highly efficient tandem mass spectrometry database searches, including real-time search workflows. However, the index can require tens of gigabytes of memory, often exceeding the free memory available on instrument acquisition computers running the search. This restricts the size of the searchable database, the variable modification space, and the number of searches that can run concurrently. To address this problem, we developed an index-pruning pipeline within the Comet database search tool using Carafe, a deep learning tool that predicts fragment ion intensities based on peptide sequences. In our approach, only fragment ion positions that are predicted to be observable are written in the index, eliminating entries that are unlikely to contribute to spectrum detection. We evaluated this approach on two search spaces in three index configurations to demonstrate that masking significantly reduced the number of fragment ion index entries and, consequently, peak search memory use. Masked searches were also faster than unmasked searches and identified a comparable number of peptide-spectrum matches. Because all prediction and masking steps are performed before searching, their cost is amortized across repeated, future searches of the same database and modification configuration, introducing no per-spectrum search overhead. The complete implementation is open source with an Apache license.

title: TCT26: Medtronic Symplicity blood pressure procedure shows significant blood pressure drops in SPYRAL AFFIRM real-world study
[Ambulatory surgery and enhanced recovery after surgery: advances in concepts and clinical practice].
source: PubMed · Zhonghua yi xue za zhi
desc: [Zhonghua yi xue za zhi] Ambulatory surgery and the concept of enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) are deeply integrated, reshaping the surgical care model. This article systematically reviews and critically analyzes advances in ERAS-driven ambulatory surgery across multiple dimensions, including its current status, the expanding scope of enhanced recovery, and future perspectives. Available evidence shows that ERAS-guided ambulatory surgery not only ensures surgical safety but also significantly shortens hospital stay, reduces medical costs, and improves patient satisfaction. In the future, technologies such as artificial intelligence, wearable devices, and telemonitoring will further promote ambulatory surgery toward individualization, comfort, and intelligence.

title: GaitFM: A Cross-Modal Foundation Model for Wearable Gait Assessment
desc: Gait assessment supports the diagnosis, monitoring, and prognosis of diverse movement-related conditions, such as neurological and musculoskeletal disorders. Recent advances in deep learning using everyday wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs) offer an accessible and low-cost approach to automated gait assessment. However, IMU measurements vary substantially across individuals, body locations, and device configurations, while existing deep learning models are typically developed using small, homogeneous datasets for specific clinical tasks, limiting their robustness and generalizability in diverse real-world contexts. Here we present GaitFM, a cross-modal foundation model for gait assessment using IMU sensors. GaitFM improves the generalizability of gait assessment by transferring knowledge from large vision models and pretraining on unlabeled IMU sensor data. We pretrain GaitFM on a large curated dataset comprising about 4,000 participants and 1.23 million gait windows across diverse clinical and daily conditions, sensor modalities, and body locations. GaitFM demonstrates strong performance across 18 gait-related tasks, including 3 gait parameter estimation tasks, 14 disease and gait abnormality detection tasks, and 1 clinical outcome prediction task. Furthermore, GaitFM generalizes across different sensor configurations and body locations, including those commonly used in clinical settings and everyday wearable devices. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of transferring visual knowledge in improving sensor-based gait assessment performance, offering a new promising pathway for addressing data scarcity in the sensor and medical domains.

title: LOTUS: lineage-aware optimal transport reconstructs continuous clonal fate dynamics
desc: Destructive sampling in single-cell sequencing obscures ancestor-descendant relationships, limiting the continuous reconstruction of cell-fate dynamics. Here we present Lineage-aware optimal transport for unbalanced single-cell dynamics (LOTUS), a framework that integrates time-resolved transcriptomic snapshots with clonal lineage information from engineered barcodes or endogenous T cell receptor clonotypes. LOTUS couples clone-level optimal transport with neural unbalanced transport to model continuous cellular state change, population growth and clonal propagation under lineage-consistent constraints. In branching simulations, LOTUS reduced lineage-inconsistent transport relative to benchmark methods, lowering off-target routing from 4.94-14.84% to 1.10%. On LARRY lineage-barcode scRNA-seq of hematopoiesis, LOTUS reconstructed branching trajectories, improved early neutrophil-monocyte fate-boundary prediction, and inferred multi-fate progenitors and fate-biased meta-clones, linking their distinct fate potentials to inferred epigenetic priming. On CellTagging scRNA-seq of fibroblast reprogramming, it distinguished reprogrammed from failed trajectories and prioritized fate-associated perturbation genes. In longitudinal scRNA-seq and TCR-seq of malaria-responsive memory (CD45RA-) CD4+ T cells, it preserved endogenous clonotype structure and reconstructed TR1 dynamics and regulatory networks. LOTUS thus converts lineage-resolved single-cell snapshots into interpretable, continuous models of fate dynamics and their regulatory programs.

title: Performance of Deep Learning Algorithms for Segmentation of Shoulder Anatomy on MRI: A Systematic Review.
source: PubMed · Journal of imaging informatics in medicine
desc: [Journal of imaging informatics in medicine] To synthesize the performance and methodological characteristics of fully automated deep learning algorithms for shoulder magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) segmentation. This systematic review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement. CENTRAL, PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore were searched from inception through July 17, 2026. The protocol specified fully automated deep learning-based pixel-wise segmentation of shoulder MRI, an expert-derived MRI-space reference standard, and quantitative segmentation metrics. Two reviewers independently screened records; unresolved disagreements were adjudicated by a senior reviewer. Overlapping datasets were linked during synthesis. Of 354 identified records, 169 duplicates were removed, 185 records were screened, and 53 full-text reports were assessed. Thirty-five reports were included (31 journal articles and 4 full conference papers; 2018-2026). U-Net-based encoder-decoder architectures predominated, with additional region-based, transformer, adversarial, and autoencoder approaches. Dice similarity coefficients ranged from approximately 0.81-0.99 for osseous targets, 0.71-0.99 for shoulder muscles, and 0.58-0.94 for tendon or tear regions; intersection-over-union values for tear or surgical-planning regions ranged from 0.45-0.83. MRI protocols and validation designs were heterogeneous, and most reports described retrospective single-center investigations. Five reports used independent external test sets; several others included multicenter images. Overlapping cohorts precluded a valid pooled participant count. Deep learning achieved high accuracy for shoulder bones and rotator-cuff muscles in selected datasets, whereas tear-region performance was more variable. Multicenter patient-level validation and standardized annotation and reporting are needed before routine clinical deployment.

title: A generative foundation model for computational brain imaging
desc: Computational brain imaging is constrained by a mismatch between increasingly diverse tasks and scarce, heterogeneous clinical data. Although existing brain foundation models transfer pretrained representations, their knowledge remains entangled within model-specific features and fixed architectures. This paper proposes BrainGFM, a generative foundation model that extends knowledge transfer beyond representation reuse through a reusable and reconfigurable brain-imaging prior. By pretraining on a corpus of about 1.3 million MRI and CT slices, BrainGFM supported task-aligned data synthesis for low-data predictive learning and task-adapted post-training for image reconstruction. Across 48 downstream tasks, BrainGFM improved segmentation and classification under limited supervision and achieved high-fidelity image enhancement across heterogeneous imaging conditions. Multicenter clinical validation involving 4,796 stroke patients across two internal and four external centers demonstrated its applicability to three clinically relevant tasks around stroke cohorts. Blinded reader assessments showed that BrainGFM-generated FLAIR images approached acquired FLAIR in overall diagnostic quality. In a human-AI collaboration study, BrainGFM assistance yielded a 14% relative improvement in mean radiologist stroke-subtyping accuracy. These findings support generative priors as a reusable foundation for heterogeneous computational brain-imaging applications.

title: Artificial intelligence-based decision support for axial spondyloarthritis integrating inflammatory and structural MRI information.
desc: [Frontiers in immunology] Axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) assessment on MRI is complicated by interpretation difficulty and by clinical variables that may be incomplete at the time of imaging. We aimed to develop an image-only deep learning framework to approximate the clinical assessment of axSpA from sacroiliac joint (SIJ) MRI, integrating fat-suppressed T1-weighted (FS T1) and short tau inversion recovery (STIR) sequences to capture structural and inflammatory information without clinical variables. This retrospective study included patients with chronic back pain who underwent SIJ MRI from January 2010 to December 2021. The treating rheumatologist's clinical diagnosis served as the reference standard. A two-stage framework integrated FS T1 and STIR features with Stage 1-derived binary bone marrow edema (BME) predictions to generate an axSpA probability. Performance in a test set was compared with the Assessment of SpondyloArthritis International Society (ASAS) definition of a "positive MRI" and the ASAS classification criteria using exact McNemar tests; discordant cases were analyzed separately. Among 291 patients (163 axSpA, 128 non-axSpA), the model achieved an AUROC of 0.9412, accuracy of 86.0%, sensitivity of 87.5%, and specificity of 84.0% in the test set (n=57). No significant paired differences in accuracy, sensitivity, or specificity were detected between the model and either ASAS comparator. In an exploratory analysis of 10 cases discordant between ASAS "positive MRI" assessment and clinical diagnosis, the model correctly classified 7 (70.0%). The model showed similar performance to the ASAS-based comparators in the test set without clinical variables, suggesting potential value as an image-based decision-support tool. External multicenter validation is needed to confirm generalizability.

title: Multimodal Prompt Learning with Dual-Granularity Contrastive Alignment for Preoperative Prediction of Lung Adenocarcinoma Invasiveness Using 3D CT
desc: Accurate preoperative prediction of lung adenocarcinoma invasiveness is important for surgical planning and individualized treatment. However, overlapping CT appearances make it challenging to distinguish invasive adenocarcinoma (IAD) from Pre-IAD lesions. We propose a multimodal prompt-learning framework with dual-granularity image-text alignment for 3D CT-based IAD classification. A 3D ResNet-CBAM encoder extracts global and spatial visual features. A frozen RadBERT backbone is adapted with separate learnable prompts for report-level and keyword-level text encoding. These prompts are initialized using semantic representations derived from real-world clinical reports. Global contrastive alignment connects whole-volume CT representations with reports generated from clinician-annotated radiological attributes to provide overall semantic supervision. A multiple instance learning-based local alignment module associates spatial CT features with vascular-focused radiological keywords, to capture local imaging characteristics potentially associated with tumor invasion. The framework jointly optimizes classification and alignment objectives, while inference requires only CT images. Experiments included 1,593 pathologically confirmed nodules. On the test set, the proposed method achieved an accuracy of 87.92%, F1-score of 87.78%, and AUC of 0.9499. Its AUC significantly exceeded that of the image-only Res-CBAM baseline with the same visual backbone (0.9297; DeLong test, p = 0.0078). Ablation analyses supported the complementary contributions of global and local alignment and the benefit of report-based prompt initialization. Qualitative visualizations showed activation within nodules and adjacent vascular structures. These findings suggest that dual-granularity radiological supervision can enhance CT-based invasiveness prediction while preserving a CT-only inference workflow.

title: Raman Spectroscopy for Glioma Diagnosis Toward Precision Neuro-Oncology: A Systematic Review.
desc: [Critical reviews in oncology/hematology] Gliomas are the most common primary malignant tumors of the central nervous system and remain difficult to manage because of diffuse infiltration and molecular heterogeneity. As glioma classification increasingly relies on molecular biomarkers, interest has grown in label-free technologies capable of providing real-time biochemical information during surgery. Although Raman spectroscopy has emerged as a promising optical approach, its diagnostic performance and translational readiness remain incompletely defined. This systematic review was registered in PROSPERO and conducted according to PRISMA 2020 guidelines. PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched for studies published between 2015 and 2025 evaluating Raman-based technologies for glioma diagnosis. Two reviewers independently performed study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment using QUADAS-2. Owing to methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesized using a SWiM-guided narrative approach. Forty-seven studies met the eligibility criteria. Across conventional Raman spectroscopy, surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy, stimulated Raman histology, stimulated Raman scattering, and multimodal platforms, Raman-based technologies consistently demonstrated strong performance for tissue discrimination, tumor margin assessment, molecular characterization, and intraoperative tissue evaluation. Recent studies increasingly integrated artificial intelligence for automated tissue classification and molecular prediction. However, substantial heterogeneity in acquisition protocols, analytical workflows, and validation strategies, together with predominantly retrospective single-center studies and limited external validation, reduced confidence in clinical generalizability. QUADAS-2 identified the greatest risk of bias in the patient-selection and index-test domains. Raman spectroscopy is evolving from an optical imaging technique into a molecular decision-support platform for precision neuro-oncology. Future clinical translation will depend on methodological standardization, prospective multicenter validation, explainable artificial intelligence, and integration into routine neurosurgical workflows.

title: State-Aware Virtual Patient Simulation for Training Psychiatrists in Challenging Clinical Scenarios
desc: Psychiatrists must be prepared to manage patients exhibiting challenging psychological states, including suicidal ideation, hallucinations, and other high-risk behaviors. However, opportunities to safely practice such interactions are limited. While recent conversational agents can simulate patients, existing approaches largely rely on large language models (LLMs) to determine patient responses, making it difficult to consistently maintain psychological state, adapt to the clinician's responses, and generate clinically plausible challenges that meaningfully test the clinician. We present a state-aware virtual patient simulation pipeline for training psychiatrists in challenging clinical scenarios. The proposed system maintains an evolving patient state throughout the interaction and orchestrates patient behavior rather than leaving response generation entirely to an LLM. At each interaction, a learning-based behavioral strategy selector determines the type and level of challenge appropriate to the current patient and clinician context. The selected strategy, patient state, clinician response, interaction history, and relevant clinical knowledge are then provided as grounded context to an LLM to generate a semantically relevant and psychologically consistent patient response. Following each session, the system analyzes the interaction and provides feedback to the clinician on their communication and management of the virtual patient.

title: Artificial intelligence for ophthalmic vessel segmentation: from multimodal imaging to clinical translation.
desc: [Frontiers in medicine] Artificial intelligence (AI)-based vessel segmentation converts color fundus photographs, scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (SLO), optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA), structural OCT, and anterior-segment images into quantitative vascular biomarkers. Strong performance within individual datasets has not consistently yielded reliable clinical measurements because errors can arise during acquisition, anatomical preprocessing, vessel extraction, biomarker calculation, and deployment. This structured narrative review compares segmentation tasks involving retinal vascular trees, OCTA capillary plexuses, the structural choroid and choriocapillaris, macular neovascularization, corneal neovascularization, and conjunctival microvasculature. We assess modern architectures in relation to vessel geometry, severe foreground-background imbalance, scale variation, crossings, and susceptibility to artifacts. The methods considered include multiscale feature pyramids, deformable and directional operators, Transformers, state-space models, diffusion approaches, and foundation models. We organize the synthesis around five evaluation levels: pixel overlap, centerline recovery, vascular topology, biomarker agreement, and clinical actionability. Public fundus and OCTA datasets are catalogued with their acquisition and annotation characteristics, and gaps in public anterior-segment vessel benchmarks are discussed. Because devices, data splits, labels, and post-processing differ substantially, reported metrics are summarized without ranking studies against one another. The review distinguishes structural OCT choroidal vascularity index from OCTA choriocapillaris flow-deficit mapping, as well as true vessel segmentation from global hyperemia grading. Clinical translation will require ocular-magnification correction, quality control of retinal layers and projection artifacts, external testing across devices and populations, out-of-distribution rejection, DICOM/PACS interoperability, prospective impact studies, and regulation as software as a medical device. We conclude that clinical utility depends on an auditable pipeline that measures structural error, biomarker uncertainty, and failure states throughout the workflow.

title: AR-RRG: Anatomy-Guided Retrieval-Driven Radiology Report Generation
desc: Radiology report generation (RRG) streamlines clinical workflows and alleviates the burden of radiologists' documentation. Standard vision-language models capture global visual cues and lack fine-grained alignment between anatomical regions and diagnostic text. Most retrieval-augmented methods retrieve complete historical reports, introducing redundant noise and severe vision-text mismatches that trigger clinically risky hallucinations and missed lesions. In this paper, we introduce AR-RRG, an anatomy-guided retrieval-driven method for the generation of radiology reports. AR-RRG consists of two core modules: the anatomy-aware self-training lesion detection network (ASLDNet) and the retrieval-driven radiology report generation (RRRG). ASLDNet leverages anatomy-aware spatial verification (ASV) and class-adaptive dynamic thresholding (CDT) via self-training, delivering accurate lesion localization to support subsequent generation. As the generative branch of AR-RRG, RRRG eliminates clinical hallucinations through dual-granularity retrieval (DR) and complements missing lesions with a neighborhood consensus (NC) mechanism. A parallel continuous visual perception (PCVP) stream converts radiographs into visual tokens through fixed medical encoding and resampling. Multi-scale text and visual features are fused, followed by LoRA-efficient large language model tuning to generate clinically consistent, visually grounded radiology reports. Extensive evaluations on MS-CXR, MIMIC-CXR, and IU X-Ray demonstrate that AR-RRG consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods across mainstream metrics. Our code will be made publicly available.

title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Developing a Future-Ready Nursing Workforce: A Systematic Review.
desc: [Journal of nursing management] Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming health care through advanced technologies that support clinical practice, education, workforce management, and decision making. As healthcare systems face growing challenges related to workforce shortages, increasing service demands, and rapid digital transformation, there is a need to understand how AI can contribute to the development of a future-ready nursing workforce equipped with the competencies required for modern healthcare environments. This systematic review aimed to examine the role of AI in developing a future-ready nursing workforce and to synthesize current evidence regarding its applications, benefits, challenges, and implications for workforce preparedness. A systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 and was registered in PROSPERO. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL, and IEEE Xplore were searched for studies published between January 2015 and February 2026. Eligible primary studies examined an identifiable AI technology or an AI-specific construct in nursing education, clinical practice, workforce development, competency development, workforce planning, or professional preparedness. Methodological quality was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool, and findings were synthesized narratively. A total of 38 primary empirical studies satisfied the AI-specific eligibility criteria. The evidence was concentrated in cross-sectional (n = 15) and qualitative (n = 11) designs, with fewer development/prototype (n = 6), mixed methods (n = 3), randomized or quasi-experimental (n = 2), and methodological (n = 1) studies. AI-supported education, clinical decision support, workforce forecasting, and competency development showed promising benefits, but much of the evidence was based on perceptions, simulations, prototypes, or single-site evaluations rather than long-term implementation. Recurrent barriers included limited AI literacy, ethical and privacy concerns, algorithmic bias, infrastructure constraints, workflow integration, and organizational readiness. AI has promising, but still uneven, potential to support a future-ready nursing workforce. Current evidence supports cautious and staged integration rather than uncritical scale-up. Standardized AI and digital competency frameworks, human oversight, governance, infrastructure readiness, and prospective evaluation of effectiveness, equity, and cost are needed before widespread deployment. title: Accounting for Irregular State Transitions through Belief Estimation in Online Medical Consultation
desc: While online medical consultation broadens access, unprompted patient disclosures and topic shifts frequently disrupt clinician inquiry, leaving clinical states progressively revealed. We characterize these dynamics using both existing evaluation metrics and task-specific interaction metrics designed in this work. Through an empirical study across 16 medical dialogue datasets, we show that authentic online interactions exhibit substantially lower contextual continuity and higher unpredictability than offline and simulated benchmarks. We propose PRISM (Policy Reasoning with Inferred States for Medicine), a framework inspired by partially observable Markov decision processes that decouples latent state estimation from action selection to address drifting dialogue trajectories. Specifically, PRISM factorizes clinical triage into belief estimation, policy optimization, and response realization. By maintaining an evolving posterior belief over consultation states and conditioning action selection on the maximum a posteriori state, PRISM advances clinical goals while accommodating patient-initiated shifts. Extensive evaluations show that PRISM substantially outperforms frontier LLMs and clinical agents, achieving a 22.40 percentage point gain in clinical decision accuracy alongside decisive improvements in response generation, surpassing the strongest baseline by 5.51 points in BERTScore_F1. Furthermore, ablation studies show that providing oracle consultation states consistently boosts response quality across all evaluated baselines by guiding their action reasoning, yielding average gains of 5.58 points in BERTScore_F1.

title: Fungal-bacterial interactions.
desc: [Current biology : CB] The study of fungal-bacterial interactions is an emerging field of biology with relevance for environmental health, medicine, and agriculture, among other sectors. The frequent co-occurrence of fungi and bacteria in many habitats has facilitated the evolution of their symbioses. Both groups are key players in host-associated microbiomes and in nutrient cycling, and these roles often intersect in dynamic ways. Interactions between fungi and bacteria can be mutualistic, commensal, or pathogenic, and they can vary in a context-dependent manner. In mutualistic interactions, fungi and bacteria can exchange nutrients, ameliorate each other's stress, enhance growth, enable dispersal, and facilitate novel niche exploration via metabolite exchange. In contrast, antagonistic interactions frequently involve competition for limited nutrients, such as iron, and active chemical warfare with secreted and bioactive compounds. Bacteria associated with fungi can occur inside of fungal cells (endosymbiotic) or on the surface of fungal hyphae (exosymbiotic). Endosymbiotic bacteria can be further differentiated into facultative symbionts, which retain the ability to enter fungal hyphae but also live independently, and obligate endosymbionts, which are always intracellular and not capable of independent life outside of hyphae. Whereas free-living bacteria can be pathogenic or mutualistic, endosymbiotic bacteria are often regarded as commensals or mutualists, although some can exhibit parasitic attributes in some conditions. A combination of molecular genetics, genomics, and microscopy has been used to study free-living bacteria. In addition to these approaches, fluorescence and electron microscopy have been used as the gold standards to study and differentiate endosymbiotic bacteria based on their intracellular location. More recently, researchers have started using systems-biology approaches to study fungal-bacterial interactions including high-throughput -omics assays. These methods produce expansive datasets that are ideally suited to artificial intelligence (AI)-based approaches to tackle long-standing questions about the basic biology and evolution of fungal-bacterial interactions. In this primer we give an overview of fungal-bacterial interactions, including their diversity, community structure, and symbiotic evolution. We highlight two research systems in particular: the intracellular endosymbionts of Mucoromycota fungi and the free-living bacteria associated with edible

title: GESTALT: Fast, Generalizable Histopathology Image Synthesis from Gene Expression with Pretrained Pathology Foundation Models
desc: Spatial transcriptomics measures gene expression while preserving where each cell sits in the tissue. The inverse, what a given transcriptomic state looks like, is less explored but equally useful: it lets researchers visualize the morphological consequence of a molecular state and interpret a spatial assay's molecular calls against real tissue structure. GeneFlow, the current state of the art on the Xenium gene expression-to-image benchmark, trains a model from scratch, incurring a high cost on every new target dataset it is applied to. We instead propose GESTALT, which reformulates gene expression-to-image synthesis as predicting a pathology foundation model's image embedding. A lightweight gene-token transformer predicts this embedding from multi-cell gene expression, and a frozen or LoRA-adapted diffusion decoder (PixCell) renders it as an image. Because this visual knowledge is reused rather than relearned, GESTALT trains in a fraction of the time. In both multi-cell and single-cell settings, our method outperforms the SoTA on perceptual metrics across all three Xenium datasets. Beyond improved image quality, GESTALT natively synthesizes at 1024 x 1024, and is evaluated in three generalization settings: zero-shot transfer across gene panels and datasets, held-out patients and disease states, and transfer across studies and tissue sources. Coupled with a statistical model of spatial expression, GESTALT also provides, to our knowledge, the first paired synthesis of cell-resolved transcriptomic fields and tissue images with explicit control over cell type, density, and composition. Code is available at https://github.com/trongnhandev1011/Gestalt.

title: Reducing radiographic retake rates with ultra-low dose pre-shots using deep learning-based noise reduction: A prospective clinical study.
